# The Rule That Charges Your Shop Before It Opens

If you want to open a café in most cities, the law tells you how many parking spaces you must provide before anyone asks whether you can afford them. These parking minimums require a fixed number of spaces per square foot of business, and many were set decades ago with little evidence behind them. They should be repealed, and small businesses have the most to gain.

Consider the arithmetic. A surface space costs roughly $5,000 to $10,000 to build, and a space in a garage can exceed $25,000. A requirement of ten spaces per 1,000 square feet for a restaurant can make the lot larger than the dining room. That cost reaches you through higher rent, or it blocks you from leasing an older storefront at all because the building lacks the spaces the code now demands. Plenty of main-street shops sit vacant for exactly this reason.

**Objection one: "My customers drive. No parking, no customers."** Removing minimums doesn't ban parking. It lets you, rather than a zoning table, decide how much your trade needs. A hardware store may keep its lot. A barber on a busy corridor may not need one. When Buffalo scrapped its minimums in 2017, new developments still included parking, just less of it, matched to actual demand.

**Objection two: "Others will skimp, and their customers will take the spaces outside my door."** This is a fair worry. The fix is managing the street, not mandating lots. Metered or time-limited parking keeps spaces turning over, so shoppers can find a spot near you. Old Pasadena returned its meter revenue to the district for lighting and sidewalk repairs. That money stayed on the same blocks where it was collected.

Minimums force every business to buy the same expensive insurance against a problem only some of them have. Ask your council to let you decide what your customers need.
